newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones given rough ride by shareholders.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones given rough ride by shareholders.

text.p: The management of Dow Jones & Co., under fire from shareholders, admitted Wednesday it had not moved quickly enough to shore up its electronic information business.

Directors at the company's annual meeting listened as shareholders lamented the fall in the stock price since 1987 and attacked plans to spend $650 million to beef up Dow Jones Markets, formerly Telerate.
"...Telerate is a bottomless pit that could take billions to turn around and even then is not a sure bet," said James Cramer, a long-time critic who owns more than 1 million shares.

Dow Jones, the publisher of the Wall Street Journal, is the world's second largest provider of news and information to financial markets, after Reuters Holdings Plc. But in recent years it has grown less fast than both Reuters and aggressive newcomer Bloomberg LP.
Dow Jones Chief Executive Peter Kann was asked by a shareholder what went wrong to allow Bloomberg LP and Reuters to outpace them.
"Looking back, we did not invest enough money in the business early enough," Kann said.
"We did not foresee the growth on the buy side. Bloomberg did and profited from it," he said.

The buy side includes investment managers at institutions such as mutual funds, while its counterpart, the sell-side, includes traders and analysts at Wall Street brokerages -- the main customers of both Dow Jones and Reuters.

Dow Jones first quarter 1997 earnings, reported last week, tumbled to $25.4 million from $37.6 million a year earlier despite a strong performance at the Wall Street Journal because of an 84 percent fall in operating profits to $7.5 million at Dow Jones Markets.
Dow Jones stock was unchanged at $39.625 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock peaked a decade ago at $56 before the 1987 crash.

Ronald Chen of the Independent Association of Publishers Employees, a union representing 20 percent of Dow Jones staff, said profits had been stagnant for a decade but management, not the market, should be blamed.
"Ten years ago Reuters and our company had the same market value, today Reuters has risen to a $20 billion value while our company remains at the $3 billion plus level," he said.

However, it was Dow Jones' attempt to catch up now, by pumping $650 million into its electronic information business -- known in the industry as "real-time" information -- over three to four years, that ignited the ire of many shareholders.
"From an outsiders point of view ... Telerate has never earned its cost of capital," said a fund manager from Gotham Partners, urging management to reconsider the investment.
Michael Price, whose funds hold around 5 percent of Dow Jones was asked what he expected of the meeting.
"Nothing. Its a family run business," he said.
The Bancroft family owns a majority of Dow Jones stock. The only shareholder proposal, to set up objective performance criteria for management, was defeated.
Price, like most critical investors, was putting his faith in new independent directors. He was hoping they would decide that a sale of Dow Jones Markets was more logical.
"That's the key to the equation," Price told Reuters. "These directors are very good business people," he said.

The three new independent directors on the 15 member board are Frank Newman, chief executive of Bankers Trust Co. ; Harvey Golub, chief executive at American Express Co. ; and William Steere, chairman of pharmaceutical company Pfizer Inc..
Newman told Reuters it was too early for him to give an opinion of Dow Jones investment plan.
